segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt sitting in for Ira Glass this week. In today's show, we've got stories of people at a moment of understanding something they could not have grasped before when they were younger-- stories from childhood, 10 years old, all the way up through old age, 79.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So let's start at the beginning. I should say that the entire premise of this show, the idea that there are certain things that do not make sense when you're young, it is flat out offensive to the people at the beginning of our story.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Have you guys ever heard the phrase, you'll understand this when you're older? Or this will make sense--

segments.speaker: Bernard
segments.text: Oh, my gosh.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Yes. A bunch of times.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I'm sitting with a half dozen sixth graders at a table in their middle school. And a small guy with glasses and a comic book name Bernard Arthur keeps shaking his head.

segments.speaker: Bernard
segments.text: I'm at the point where I'm used to it now, you know? Because they say it lots of times. And it's not only from my mom. It's from her friends, from adults, and from everybody. So I'm just really sick of it.

segments.speaker: Bernard
segments.text: To be honest, to be completely honest--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Be completely honest.

segments.speaker: Bernard
segments.text: I know-- we all know mostly everything about life.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wait, so you don't believe that phrase at all?

segments.speaker: Bernard
segments.text: It's not like we know everything, but we know mostly what adults think we don't know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Bernard just feels like that stuff you think I'm not ready for? I am. Let's talk.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: At least three kids at the table raise a finger and politely say, "um, I'd like to add to that." They've all got examples of questions they asked recently that were met with some version of, you'll understand later. A brief selection, why do you smoke? Why did she commit suicide? Why do I have to go to school?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What does it mean to hit puberty? Who is puberty? And why would you hit her?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How do you say butt hole in Spanish? It's a pretty broad range, right?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A girl named Samantha Boome says sometimes you don't even have to ask a question to be shut down with the "you'll understand later," even if it's not those exact words. Like the other night, she came into the kitchen. And her mom and grandpa were talking in loud voices, maybe they were fighting.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: And I was like, "hey, can I get the cookie jar to get some cookies?" And they're like, "no. You can't. You'll learn when you get older."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's saying, you'll learn when you get older.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: I'm like, but I was just asking for a cookie. She's like, "I'm not in the mood right now. I'm talking to your grandfather." I'm like, "oh, my god. But, Mom, chill out." And then I had to walk out of the room. I'm like, sheesh. Now I can't get a cookie.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I think to kids, this phrase can feel both dismissive and like we, the adults, are abdicating our responsibility, giving up on even trying. Like Jasper Pena says, when he asks what seems like a pretty simple question, sometimes grown-ups say--

segments.speaker: Jasper
segments.text: Probably only God knows the answer. I don't know the answer, but I know that God knows it. And I get frustrated when they say that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Jasper
segments.text: Because you're like, I know that they know the answers. And something's telling me they know the answers.

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: You can't have a conv-- you can, but you can't like physically have a conversation with him and ask him the question. That's like--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: With God?

segments.speaker: Samantha
segments.text: Yeah. It's better if you ask an actual person because they will actually give you an answer because they know the people, instead of God.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She wants an actual person. These kids want answers. Well, today on our show, we have answers. Or rather, we have people arriving at the answers themselves, with or without the help of others. People looking ahead in time for clues of what's to come, and looking back at the remarkable facts that they somehow missed. We're going to travel from childhood on up, stopping at all the points where people do understand, finally. We've got Sasheer Zamata from Saturday Night Live . Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Act One, Adolescence. When the biggest thing that does not make sense is often just the immediate future and how you're going to get through it. Here's Hillary Frank.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: There's this kid in my town. We'll call him Ben. A few years ago, Ben was starting high school, and he turned 15. He asked his parents if he could throw a party. They said yes, but if we see any alcohol, we're shutting it down. Ben's like, fine.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: The day of the party he takes a walk with his five closest guy friends. They're sort of his planning committee. They tell him they're going to text invites to, like, 30 people. Mostly, they're other geeky guy friends. Also, their friends tell him, we're going to invite some popular girls.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: They were basically like, you'll be the man for a week if you do this.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: They all go back to Ben's house. And the popular girls, they're actually the first to show up.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: And then half an hour in, I make the biggest mistake of my life up to this point when one of the girls, one of the "popular," quote, unquote, girls asked me what my address was. And in my mind-- in my freshman mind-- they were getting picked up. They were already getting picked up, like they were telling their parents to come get them. Because that's what asking for an address meant to me at this time, like, completely innocent thing.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Four or five more girls asked for Ben's address. Of course, these kids are not calling their rides. They're texting his address to all their friends.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: So the party slowly starts growing. And then a bunch of older kids show up. Then Ben hears banging outside on his garage door. Suddenly, there's a bunch of upperclassman everywhere.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: They were coming up from behind, in the flanks, and the front. And people were looking in the bushes and crawling to all the different windows, looking in, seeing who's in there. I'd say about half of them are people I know. But it's the people I know that I would never want them to come. And it's kids that bullied me in middle school and elementary school. And they're calling people inside trying to get in through the back.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: This thing that was happening to Ben, it's straight out of every memorable teen party movie. His little birthday celebration was crashed. But what was happening here is different from those movies in one key way, a way that seems to be specific to my town and towns nearby.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Upperclassman conspire to target freshman parties, freshman like Ben. And at these parties, the parents are home. The older kids, though, they are not deterred by parents. Parents can be yelling at them to get off their lawn, and the kids will pretend to go, but really they are sneaking in around back. And once they get in, they tell the younger kids, this is our party now.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: This is so common in my town that parents are calling it parasiting. They try to deal with it themselves. They try not to call the cops. They don't want their kids to be humiliated, but it can get overwhelming.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: One mom I talked to got a call from a friend while this was going on at her house. The friend warned her, they'll find a way around you. You can't stop them.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: It's like a military raid. It's like D-Day. It's like any sort of multifaceted attack where the base is just completely up for grabs and anything goes. And all morals are just thrown out the window completely.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: The party has more than doubled in size. There are now 70 kids at Ben's house. His mom's on the lawn, calling out kids by name and threatening to tell their parents that they were here. His dad is getting into it with some kid who's trying to push his way inside the house.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Ben looks around. He's surrounded by strangers-- older strangers. They're chugging beer. They're on their phones explaining to their friends the best method of breaking into the house. Ben's standing right next to them as they're doing this. Someone turns up the music, and a corner of the basement suddenly becomes a dance floor. The toilet is full of beer cans.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: There is this girl who's chugging something. I don't remember. I told her, "can you please not do this?" And she looked at me and in the most rude, sarcastic voice said to me, "like, thanks for the hospitality," and turned around and just trudged back in a different direction.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: After about an hour, kids started calling their friends telling them to not bother coming in. This party was lame. And as quickly as they came, they left.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: I was freaking out the entire time. I'm still freaking out about it just thinking about it. It was horrible. It was pretty scarring.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: For the rest of Ben's freshman year, he was terrified of older kids. He'd go to parties, but he hated when they'd get blown up. He hated when the older kids would take their control away.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: But Ben grew up. He's a senior now. And he says--

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Somewhere between sophomore and junior year, I just decided I was completely comfortable with showing up with my friends to random people's houses and treating them with the same lack of respect that I was treated with when I was in ninth grade because that's what you do.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: He started getting those texts saying there's a party happening at so-and-so's and house. Let's blow it up. He started getting invited more and more till eventually the text would just be an address, nothing else. But he'd know what it meant.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: [YELLING]

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: This sound comes from a video that Ben sent me that one of his friends shot at a party.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: All the (PRETENDING TO YELL) "yo's" and "look at that"-- it's all just like you're kind of in awe where you've ended up in that moment. "That's that kid from my biology class. Like, oh, my god. Come over here."

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: That's one of the things Ben told me he loves about crashing freshman parties. You never know who's going to show up. It's like nobody's invited, so everybody's invited.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Also, it's super convenient. There's always a party because you don't have to wait for your friend's parents to go out of town. And Ben says it's thrilling, what it takes to get into the house -- the Black Ops -- getting intel from your friends inside about which entryways are guarded and which are clear.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: But yes, it is like a stealth mission a lot of the times, seeking out which route is the most efficient form of entry. Next time, maybe I'll bring a notepad and sketch out my ideas or draw a blueprint of the house because that's basically what we're doing.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: And it feels OK to you, even though that happened to you when you were a freshman?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Well, let me put it this way. And this is kind of not the best mentality. But if I don't show up, nothing is going to change. So I'm going to show up like everyone else because me not going isn't going to stop anything from happening.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Well, in reality, I never pictured myself as one of those kids. We would always be like, wow, those kids are such jerks. We'll never be like them. But once you're older, you just-- your mindset turns into, I am one of the older kids. I have power over the younger kids. And that is a new form of intimidation.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Ben spent two hours at my house sitting on my couch answering my questions. It all seemed to be getting a little too real for him. He was struggling to make sense of the boy he'd been and the man he'd become. By the end, he was lying down, rubbing his head.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Wow, I'm really just-- I'm really just conflicting myself everywhere.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Ben started philosophizing, talking about all the ways you change so quickly during those years in high school. He told me there are three phases when it comes to blowing up parties. Phase one is when you get blown up. You're an innocent, naive little freshman. Phase two, you're doing the blowing up. And it is deliciously sadistic. Phase three, you're kind of over it.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: And I realized that that's just like the circle of life in high school. It's like at a certain point you reach a sort of wise, old sage status because I guess we're getting more mature now. But there is a gap between your immaturity and your maturity where you're still immature but you think you aren't.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: So you take the authority, and you say, I have the right to show up at this person's house because I'm old. And I'm 16 years old. And I'm going to be applying to college soon. And I grew a mustache a few days ago.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: What would you say now to your freshman self?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: I would say, don't let other people decide who's going to come to your house. Or I would say, don't have a party ever.

segments.speaker: Hillary Frank
segments.text: Ben's got a few months left in his senior year. He's more choosy about parties these days, but he says he'll still go because he's got to do this while he still can. In the fall, he'll start college. And he's pretty sure the parties there will be more sophisticated. And by that, I mean he won't have to break and enter. He'll walk through the front door like a real grown-up.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hillary Frank is host of the wonderful parenting podcast The Longest Shortest Time . It's on the Earwolf network. longestshortesttime.com.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Act Two, Grown.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Sasheer Zamata is a comedian. She's on Saturday Night Live . She does a lot of her own stand-up. And like a lot of comics, Sasheer uses the stage to rehash real things that happened to her and try to make sense of them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But recently, Sasheer felt like there was more to figure out about the stuff she was saying on stage. A warning-- the thing that kicked this off for her involves a nasty word, a racial slur. And there is no way for her to tell what happened without saying it a bunch of times. Sasheer's story about this starts with her on stage.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I got called the n-word once in my life, thankfully. And it happened in such a stereotypical way, you won't believe it. I was walking down the street in Cocoa Beach, Florida. Of course, it happened in Florida.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: And I was walking with another friend who's also a black woman. And this dirty pickup truck comes barreling down the road towards us. And it had a Confederate flag vanity plate.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: And this very red-faced man-- that's the politically correct way to say it.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: A very red-faced man leans his face out the window. And he has these reflector sunglasses that strap to your head. And he yells at us. And he goes, "y'all niggas need to take yo' black asses back to Africa." And keeps going.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: And I was like, were we punked? He had all the things.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: He had all the racist trappings. Like he did it on purpose. Like he went into a store and was like, "I need to look at as racist as I feel."

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I've been telling a joke for a couple of years now. And it always gets a laugh. But when it happened, it was really scary. And it must have really shook me up because I did something I rarely do when I'm upset. I called my mom. And she actually found it funny.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: You laughed at me. I was crying. And I called you from the car. And I was like, they called me a nigger. That's never happened to me. And you were like, please.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Every day of the eighth grade I was a different flavor of nigger. Nigger all day long. Nigger on the bus. Nigger in the bathroom.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: From kids?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: From the kids, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I was like 20 or 21. That was the first I ever heard that or, like, it's ever been used to me. It's at least nice that--

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: It took that long.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: --it took that long,

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: But, yeah, it still doesn't feel good.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: No, it does not feel good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Up until that point, I hadn't really thought about the fact that my mom got called the n-word all the time when she was younger. But my mom would often drop little tidbits of information like that. And like most kids, I ignored them because she's my mom. And her life before being my mom didn't really concern me. But I did notice some of her patterns when I was a kid.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: There are little things that I remember from my childhood. Like I remember she does not love white people. I mean, I'm sure she'd like you guys if she met you.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: You guys are fine. But it would come out in little ways. It wouldn't be crazy overt, but I remember little instances happening when I was younger. Like there was one time we were in the car. She was driving, and I was in the passenger seat.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: And she stopped to let this old, white couple to pass in front of her. And she lets out this deep sigh like, ehh, white people. And I was like, uhh. They're not even talking to us right now. What's the issue? And she goes, memories. And that's where the conversation stopped.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The conversation stopped there because she never went into those memories. And I also never asked about them. I just assumed that my mom said things like that because she was old-school or close-minded. But I'm getting older. And I'm thinking about race more. I'm talking about it more in my act. And I thought, I should talk to my mom about this stuff. Why does she hate white people?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Until a few months ago, I knew very little about what she went through. I knew that in the '60s, my mom became one of the first black students to integrate a white junior high school in Forrest City, Arkansas. It was a big deal. She was part of history. And that's something I figured she'd be proud of.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: No, I didn't feel like it was a good thing. We never had a choice in the matter.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: When she says "we," she means her and her siblings. It was her mom who had the choice. I didn't know it was an option for families, that they got to choose whether they'd desegregate schools. I just thought some law was passed, and everyone agreed to go for it. But my grandmother basically forced my mom and several of her siblings to join the civil rights movement as pre-teens and go to a school where they weren't wanted.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: She had said that the reason that she wanted her kids to go to the white school was that she did not want her children to be afraid of white people. But I'm thinking, that's your problem. You're afraid of white people. We didn't get the opportunity to develop how we thought about it.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Did you ever talk to your mom about stuff she went through? Do you know what she went through as a black woman in the South growing up?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: She was very close-mouthed. So no, she wouldn't talk about it.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Did you ever ask?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Yes. And you get told it ain't your business.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: It ain't your business?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: It ain't your business. I quote, "it ain't your business."

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Seems like not talking about this particular subject is a tradition in our family. When I asked my mom why she never talked to me about this, she said she didn't want me to inherit her feelings about white people and she wanted me to come to my own conclusions. But the more questions I asked, especially about school, the more I felt like she didn't want to talk about it because it's still really painful to her.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: So then you were just thrust into this all-white environment?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: What was your first day like? Do you remember?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: We get lots of instructions. Do not argue with them. Do not antagonize them. Hold your tongue.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: There was a lot of cussing at us while we were sitting on the bus. And Mama had told us, sit in the front of the bus so in case something happens, the bus driver is a witness. Well, he was just a witness to us getting cussed out every day. He did nothing.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: When we get off the bus, we stood outside the window of the office so if anything happened, then they could witness something happening to us. The person I remember standing in the window was Coach Collier, who later became the principal. So he witnessed the kids throwing rocks at us.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: I remember I had on a white blouse, a houndstooth vest, and a black skirt, and had my cute little white bobby socks. And I remember looking down at my legs and how the rocks had pelted them. And one had broke blood.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: And some kid, I guess he pulled out a banana. He threw a banana. And it landed on my houndstooth vest. And I never got that stain out.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Being in junior high, no matter who you are, it's hard. It just sucks. People are mean.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: And so I started asking her questions about this. Like, what was it like? And my mom said, think of it like Mean Girls, but they're racist. And I was like, no.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Like that's the analogy where I fully understood. I was like, oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: That's too mean.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Did you make any friends?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: When I was in eighth grade, we sat in alphabetical order. And so the girl in front of me, her last name started with S also. So she was new to the school, too. So we were both new. And so--

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: This was a white girl?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: She was a white girl. I was the only black in the class. She became my friend. And she was real smart. And I was real smart. But I guess we were too friendly.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: There was a class for kids that were extremely smart. But I didn't think she was any smarter than I was. But they pulled her out and put her in that class. And I will always believe they did that because we were too close. You could just see their face change if another white person came into the room or down the hall. It's like, they turned their head like, who's watching me talk to this black person?

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: When I learned about the civil rights movement in school, I got a pretty truncated version of it. I remember learning about the Little Rock Nine. And I saw that famous picture of them entering Central High School surrounded by US soldiers. And then desegregation happened. And now we get to use the same bathrooms. That's pretty much all I got.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I didn't know about what those kids went through on a day-to-day basis. But my mother, on the other hand, did. The school she eventually went to was just a little over an hour away from Little Rock. And she was paying very close attention to what was going on there.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: In Little Rock, the Little Rock Nine, when they integrated Central High School, nine black kids. And they had a lady named Daisy somebody.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: That's Daisy Bates, the head of the Arkansas chapter of the NAACP at the time.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: She would walk these kids to school every day. She would listen to them. And I mean, this is stuff I read in the newspaper, how she was sympathetic to what they were going through. And all day long, people were calling them the nigger. Or the teacher calling the nigger. Or the kids calling them niggers.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: In Ebony magazine, we would read this how sympathetic she was to them. And they had somebody to talk to. We didn't get that.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: To be clear, the Little Rock Nine were as viciously persecuted as any black students at the time. They were spat on, verbally and physically abused, attacked with fire and acid. But my mom still envied them because in her mind, those kids had access to the one thing that would have made her own situation more bearable. They had the ear of a caring adult.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: What was your relationship with your mom like?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: She had lots of kids. She had seven kids. She always made me feel like I was the runt of the litter.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: I was dark. I had really tight, kinky hair. I wasn't high-yellow like a couple of my sisters. I did not have long hair like a couple of my sisters. So I was black. I was chunky, dunky, dusty.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: She favored the lighter kids or wanted you guys to have--

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: She treated them differently.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: What her mother was teaching her was the same thing her country was teaching her, that her blackness was less valuable.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: If she's buying cute little dresses for all of her daughters, I shouldn't be the one that didn't get the dress and have to wait till my fat sister outgrew it and then I get it. I shouldn't be the one that when it's time to comb hair, make their hair look cute. And then when she gets to me and she's tired, she just throws a few plaits on my head and they're going every which a'way. I started combing my own hair when I was like sixth grade because I knew she was not go put herself out to make me look good. So I had to figure it out myself.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Of all the stuff we talked about, this is the part that made me the most sad. She feels the way she does about white people because white people were so terrible to her. And I get that. But there's something else going on. She's mad at her mom for putting her in that situation, forcing her to go to a place where white people could treat her that way.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Where I went to school, where I live, the job I have-- all those things are a direct result of desegregation. My life would have been totally different otherwise. And listening back to the recording of our conversation, I couldn't believe how many times I asked her if she was proud of her contribution.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Do you look at that time and think about how you've helped change things in America? Do you see it as a--

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: No. No.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Do you feel like you affected future generations?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: No. It was going to happen anyway. It's just that we get tortured in the process.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: So you just would have rather not have been a part of it.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Correct. It was all very unfortunate.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Well-- I don't know. I mean, I'm-- it's not all very unfortunate. It's actually very fortunate, like a lot has changed. I--

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Yeah, a lot has changed. But for that small group of people who went through this process, we got caught in the crossfire.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: So if you could go back in time, you wouldn't even do it?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: It would be so easy for my mom to just say yes, even one time. People who weren't even in the civil rights movement claim that they were a part of the civil rights movement. I get that this was a hard period in her life. But I figured she could at least see how it benefited me.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I went to school with all sorts of kids. And kids did give me trouble. But it wasn't the white kids.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: There was like a field day or something outside. And I was in the circle of white girls. And then I went over to the circle of black girls. And this one girl turned around, boxed me out of the circle, and was like, "why don't you go back and play with your little white friends?"

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: And I cried instantly. I went to the curb by myself, just cried. And my white girlfriends came over. And they were like, what's wrong? And I was like, get away from me.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: This is your fault. And then my black girlfriends came over. And they're like, what's wrong? And I was like, Star made me cry. And I explained the whole thing. And then they were like, she has no right to say that. You can hang out with whoever you want.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: That was the first time I encountered a thing where someone was like, you can't hang out with a certain group of people, even if it's your own group of people. But, yeah, there was always that separation but not the way my mom had experienced.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: My mom even asked me one day. She was like, are you afraid of black people because I primarily had a lot of white friends. Which really screwed me up because my mom's black. And I was definitely afraid of her.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [AUDIENCE LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: One time you asked me if I was scared of black people. Do you remember that?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Uh-uh.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I don't know when it was or why. I mean, I'm assuming I was in middle school or elementary school or something. But yeah, you said-- you asked, "are you afraid of black people?" And I--

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: What did you say?

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I said, no. But I think-- I assumed that question came because I mostly had white friends. And I was like, does she think I don't want to hang around black people? Kind of gave me a little complex.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I felt a little paranoid that I had so many white friends, like it was a bad thing. Not just because of you. You weren't the only person to do that. But I wasn't expecting someone in my household to also do what the bullies at my school were doing.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: It's not like I was-- did I say it more than once?

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: No, but once is really all you need to do it. I know you didn't mean to hurt me or make me feel bad, but that's what happened.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: There's a lot of stuff that parents say that--

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Yeah, it's--

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: --they don't realize is going to affect their kids like that.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Tell me about it. I get-- mm.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Do you have an example? You don't have to get into it i you don't want to.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: How do you feel about me asking you these questions?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: I'm glad you open to it because I didn't get this with my mother. And I'm glad you're curious about me. But my mother wouldn't let me be curious about her.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: My mom and I have never had the closest relationship. She and my dad split up when I was nine. And at some point, I started to focus a lot of my anger over their divorce onto her. She was always very strict with me. So we fought a lot.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Eventually, I went away to college and the tension eased up a bit. But that's mostly because we talked less. Now that I've gotten older and sat through my fair share of therapy, I've been trying to let some of that resentment go. And I'm trying to think of my mother more as a whole person.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: I am a person.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I know. But for a long time, I didn't think so.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: How do you feel about our relationship?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: I don't know. We don't really get to spend very much time. Since you've moved to New York, we don't have any deep conversations anymore. So I'm not sure how I feel about it because I can't get my hands on you.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I don't remember us having too many deep conversations.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Well, teenagers, they don't.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Well, they can.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: You know, like most single parents, I had a lot on my table, trying to maintain a job, trying to raise kids, dealing with legal drama with my ex. My plate was full. And you're doing all this stuff at school. And you're getting your good grades. And you had your own thing going.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Yeah, I did.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: But I do feel like I like, I guess, felt a separation or felt like, I guess, resentment for you having your own thing and me having my own thing.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Oh, that's a teenager thing.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I don't know if it is.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Well, I remember when I was a teenager, and I was most of the time mad at my mother.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: But you stayed mad at your mother for the rest of her life. Do you see any parallels between your relationship with your mom and our relationship?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Not at all.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Even though we still don't agree on most things, at least we're talking. That's new. I like it.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Did I ever tell you I dated a white guy?

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: No, you did not.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: What? When was this?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: After I got out of college, I was living in Little Rock. And I was dating this white guy.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: What'd he look like? Was he tall?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: No, he was not.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: He was just-- just a good Jewish boy.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Jewish?

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.text: Whoa. You dated a short Jew?

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: Yes, I did.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Wow. That-- I did not expect that at all. I just assumed-- because Papa's 6'5", so I was like, I just assumed you liked tall guys. That's cool. I have a lot of short, Jewish friends.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She told me that they dated for three months, and then she dumped him because of her mom. Her uncle saw her out one night with him.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: And he said, "you dating a white man? I'm going to call your mama and tell her what you doing up here." So when we got home that night, I was done with him.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Ivory
segments.text: I was just not that into him to think that this was worthy of a conversation I wanted to have with my mother.

segments.speaker: Sasheer Zamata
segments.text: I get that. It's never easy to figure out what conversations to have with your mother.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Sasheer Zamata, you can see her on television on Saturday Night Live.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Coming up, I use my platform as a radio show host to ask a question I have been wanting to ask for years-- from WBEZ Chicago, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's This American Life . I'm Chana Joffe-Walt sitting in for Ira Glass. Our show today is about things that make more sense when you're older. We've arrived at middle age, when a person begins to wonder, will this make sense when I'm older? Any of it? The choices I'm making, the work I'm doing, the place I live, how I'm spending my time, and how I'm not spending my time. That's one I think about a lot.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: There's a letter in my desk at work. It's a little over the top, but it gets its point across. My four-year-old wrote it with the assistance of his babysitter. It reads, "Dear mommy, I don't want you to go away again. Love, Jacob."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So am I doing this right, making the right choices? And I'm going to regret these choices in 20 years in my 50s? I think a sort of classic way people try to answer this question is to find someone in their 50s who's living it and ask them. I've got one right nearby, same line of work.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How does it feel to be on that side of the mic?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Awful.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Does it really?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Feels fine.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Ira agreed to talk to me before he got on a plane last week. So here we are. Act Three: Middle Age. And we're talking about the choices Ira's made. Ira describes his 30s this way.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Every moment, I was either working or asleep. Like those were the two things I did and didn't have a problem with it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I have noticed recently that you do do some things that are not just working.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yes, that's definitely true.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I remember you told me when you were hanging out with someone-- or you were going out to dinner and you said something like, yeah, I've started to try this new thing called friends recently.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (LAUGHING) Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's really-- it's cool.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's amazing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah, it's fun.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, it's really fun.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But that was two years ago, Ira. What happened before then?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I had friends who I wouldn't see that often, people I liked, but we wouldn't see each other, you know?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, the fact is I definitely do schedule all kinds of things now that I never would have five years ago, or 10 years ago, like during the week at night at 7 o'clock or 8 o'clock. And then I go do them. And--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why did you start doing that?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For fun.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My own amusement. I'm normal in that way. I wanted to see people. There's people I like. I wanted to see them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is that a thing that you wish you had done earlier?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It is?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. Like I wish I'd created more space for myself and I wasn't working all the time, for sure. But I don't want it enough that I'd do anything about it. You know what I mean? So then, really, how much do I want it? I want it when I see it. I think that seems good. But then in practice-- what's the thing-- what are the questions that you're asking yourself that are leading to this?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I'm not asking these questions all the time, but fairly regularly there is a moment where I step back. And I'm like I don't know if in 20 years or 30 years I'm going to be like that's what I should have been doing when I was in my 30s, when my kids were little, when my parents were still alive.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah, I guess it's not just moments. I have it a lot. I have it a lot. Those don't seem to be questions for you. It seems like-- I don't know. I didn't know you when you were in your 30s. But right now, it seems like you are very singularly directed. And you don't have the anxiety of all the other questions.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I don't.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you ever have that?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I mean, you're in a different situation because you have kids, you know?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But you're wondering, was I plagued by doubt? And I wasn't. You think about this all the time. And I never think about this. And I never really did think about this.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah. I can't imagine deciding the only thing I want to do is work and sleep. I totally can't imagine that. No, I would miss things.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: See, when you say this, this is-- this gives me this feeling of like, oh, wait. I'm more of a weirdo than I thought in this way which I don't usually think of myself at all. But I still am glad for the choice I made.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I feel like what I am getting from all of this is that you and I have many things in common. And we are extremely different human beings.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And that makes me actually the very worst person to ask this advice from. I'm too different from you to give you any advice. I mean, the thing that's different for you is a desire for free time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Which you don't have. You didn't have.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (LAUGHING) No. No, I didn't.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Ira Glass is the host of this show, just not this week.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Act Four: Old Age. So we begin when you're little. And there are things you do not know. You can't understand. And then you grow up, and you get it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We fall in love. This is love. Or someone tells you what "hooker" means. I remember that vividly. Stuff eventually makes sense.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This last story, it's about what happens after that, long after that. It's about a man named Carl Duzen. Carl was diagnosed with Alzheimer's a year and a half ago at age 79. So after decades of adulthood, it is suddenly appropriate for a 40-year-old doctor to ask him questions like, can you tell me who the president is? Or, do you remember your name?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Carl goes to the doctor, he always goes with his wife Susan. He always hates going. And he always knows his name.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: So one of the questions that you should always ask, make a picture, basically, of a clock at such and such a time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It says in words "draw a clock"?

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Yes, the round face.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I see.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Could you draw an analog clock with the time 11:20?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Susan, Carl's wife, tells me one day recently, she drove Carl to his appointment. Carl went in. And Carl tells me he waited there, pencil in hand, the tester waiting next to him, asking him, "draw a clock."

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: So I got a piece of paper. No matter what I-- I just-- I couldn't-- I couldn't do it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl tried again. He looked up at the tester, back down toward his page. Tester, his pencil.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: So, look at that and yeah, I can't do it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He can't do it. Carl got a graduate degree in physics. He studied motion, electromagnetism. He spent a lot of his life deep in the study of space and time of numbers. He taught physics and mathematics for years. So this particular failing was unnerving.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Why is this so difficult? Why is that so hard? It's clocks. Why is that so hard?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Carl talks, his wife Susan is completely still, listening, hanging on the details so she doesn't miss anything, jumping in with words when they're needed. She's a full head taller than Carl. Their favorite joke, as Susan says, I almost overlooked him. And then he jumps in the air so she can see his face.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Carl says things lately that don't have much basis in reality, Susan respectfully raises two questioning eyebrows, leaves it at that. As he's describing the trouble of the clock, Susan assures Carl he's not alone. The clock thing comes up in her support group for spouses of people with dementia.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: In the support group, people would talk about how, oh, my husband has an appointment next week with the doctor. So he's been busy practicing the clock. Oh, yeah, the clock. Oh, my husband never gets it.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Well, because it's so universal. There it is.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: It's the time. And now suddenly, you can't manage it. Ack.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: And so, I just said, OK. So what I did is got a piece of paper. I just sat down. Where is it? Let's--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you want me to follow you?

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: No, I'll bring it. I'll bring it back.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl starts looking around for something. Goes in the kitchen. He seems to be lost. And then goes upstairs. Eventually, he comes down with a wooden box. Inside, it's felted with drafting tools.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What do you have there?

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: So, I got a piece of paper. I got out the tool that I have for doing this kind of work.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So that's like a compass? It looks like the sort of compass I used in math in elementary school.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah. So I thought, OK, I'm going to-- I sat down with it for just about an hour.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: To be clear, not necessarily to draw a clock, but to figure out why he couldn't draw a clock.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: And I finally realized that the problem is superposition of three--

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Types.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: --types.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl has drawn a very precise circle, split it into twelfths, and scrawled the words "superposition of three types" in tiny letters in the corner of the page. He explains, with Susan's help, there are three layers of information here. There's the hours that are represented from 1 through 12, even though there are 24 hours in a day.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: But then, there's the second layer, which is the minutes. And a 1 represents not a 1 anymore, but 5 minutes. And a 2 represents 10.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But Carl adds, after that layer is the second hand, which is now measuring 1 through 60 seconds.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Superposition of three types.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Types because you have three different elevations that you have to get together to make the information.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl sat with his tools and his paper and his physicist's desire to decompose the problem before him. And he took apart each element of the clock until it made sense to him, the three layers, the fact that the eye goes to the larger minute hand first and your brain has to override that to focus on the smaller hour hand, which is actually more important even though it's smaller and not the first thing you see.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then you're supposed to move to the longer minute hand. But don't be tricked because the second hand is also longer but it's skinnier. And by the end of all this, I just feel like, what the hell, clock? I can't believe this is the system we have for telling time. It's insane. It's a miracle anyone can ever just glance at their wrist and capture information, something Carl works very hard at.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: So and the brain-- the brain is in there trying desperately, of course, to get hold all of these things at the same time to respond to. And it's just dead hard. And then when I did this I figured, oh, that's why it's so hard.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Your brain can't help you draw a clock, but you used your brain to figure out why your brain can't help you draw a clock.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Yeah, that's kind of the way it is. I felt like that I got something back that I had lost. But not that I could do it easily for a while, but that I at least understood why I have was having trouble.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And that felt like--

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: And that had-- it had meaning. And it had the structure.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Instead of just feeling like this is a random thing that I now suddenly can't do.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Huh.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: And it isn't easy. It is difficult. And so I felt better about myself. Got perky. More perky.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A dementia diagnosis is being told you are now no longer going to understand things as you get older. For the first time in your life, the chronological forward march of knowledge will begin to reverse itself. But Carl is understanding things he never knew before. And this is the case with lots of people with dementia.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Through meeting Carl and other people, I talked to a woman who forgot how to make coffee. And then she broke down the steps involved so she could do it again. A guy who re-learned to use his cell phone. That's something Carl has also done.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl knows way more about a clock than most of us only because he forgot how to draw one. You learn what you need to know when you need to know it. Carl tells me proudly now that he understands the superposition of three types, he can use that to read a watch again. Susan raises her eyebrows skeptically at this, but says nothing.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: From the time that I was told that I had Alzheimer's to now, the things that I had let go of because kinds of things in physics that I used to teach I can't even tell you what it is. That's gone. For a while, I couldn't use my computer, remember how to use it. And now I can go with a clock--

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Watch.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Watch.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Can you tell the time?

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: On this one, it's really tough. But here it is.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: You want to look at mine?

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE] OK, here's where it--

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Here, Carl, look at mine.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl's wearing a watch, but it's small. And he doesn't seem to know how to deal with the fact that it's covered by part of his sleeve. Susan pulls out her gold watch, which has a much larger face.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: OK. So you're looking around for information. You would go for this because that's the most important thing. It looks like it. It's the biggest one.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're pointing to the second hand.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Yes. And then there's this little bitty one over here.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: The short stubby one.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: The short stubby one. It's the smallest little thing. It's that little piece, you see? And that's the hour one. That's the one, hour by hour, that does the whole thing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You have to think through each of those steps every time you look at a watch?

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: OK, so this is-- well, here we are with the little piece. And now we are at-- let's see-- 12, 1--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Carl stops talking and is staring intensely at the watch. Susan looks very nervous. We are all leaning in. Later, I will realize that here is where I stopped breathing. Carl spends a while on that hour hand and then starts counting by fives in a whisper around the face of the watch.

segments.speaker: Susan
segments.text: Yeah, that's fantastic.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did that feel like?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [CLAPPING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: It's good. It's good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you worry-- so now you have this level of analysis that helps how know how to read a clock by thinking about what is involved in reading a clock, do you worry that you're going to forget this?

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: Sure. That's why I have to do this. There's no path back.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: There's no path back to a day when you used to be able to draw a clock using-- without having to think about it.

segments.speaker: Carl Duzen
segments.text: There's no path back.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: There are a lot of things that make sense when you're older, as in a grown-up. And then there are things that make sense when you're actually getting old, when you start to make sense of losing things. That is what I'm sure most of us cannot fully grasp until we get there ourselves, to know-- to really know-- there is no path back.
